source.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
source.authors: Aaron Mueller; Atticus Geiger; Sarah Wiegreffe; Dana Arad; Iv'an Arcuschin; Adam Belfki; Yik Siu Chan; Jaden Fiotto-Kaufman; Tal Haklay; Michael Hanna; Jing Huang; Rohan Gupta; Yaniv Nikankin; Hadas Orgad; Nikhil Prakash; Anja Reusch; A. Sankaranarayanan; Shun Shao; Alessandro Stolfo; Martin Tutek; Amir Zur; David Bau; Yonatan Belinkov

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether standard hidden-vector dimensions (neurons) can serve as features for locating task-relevant causal variables, using interchange-intervention scores rather than attribution graphs. This bears conceptually on V5's claim about neurons as analysis units, but does not reproduce its attribution-graph method.
record.gate_note: The paper's results about neuron-dimension features are included below. Circuit-localization scores and results for PCA, SAE, DAS, and full-vector methods are not separate rows: they do not measure the neuron-dimension method itself. The paper also reports model-performance numbers and circuit scores, but those do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: V5 is tested only by the circuit-localization track, which the record omits. That track builds neuron-level node circuits (NAP, NAP-IG; 'we always run NAP at the neuron granularity') in the models' own neurons, with no replacement model. It scores how faithfully they reproduce task behaviour (CMD/CPR, Tables 2, 14–16). The record's DBM rows measure something else: alignment of neuron dimensions to hypothesised causal variables. They do not measure whether neuron circuits explain behaviour, so they belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right but incomplete. The authors also conclude that, for circuit localization, attribution (EAP-IG-inputs) and mask-optimisation methods perform best and node-level circuits do poorly. For causal variables they conclude that DAS is best, DBM on neurons is a strong baseline, and SAE/PCA features fail to improve on neurons, challenging SAE utility.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses supervised or unsupervised feature alignment with causal-model interchange interventions, rather than auditing neuron poles or constructing the claim's attribution graphs.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies by task and causal variable; the paper reports especially weak results for the arithmetic carry variable and weaker RAVEL results for Llama-3.1 than Gemma-2. It also reports best-layer scores alongside averages across layers.

fits_no_version.finding: DBM on standard neuron dimensions localises task causal variables well on MCQA/ARC answer tokens (best layer 99–100) but weakly on carry and RAVEL country. SAE features (whose interventions include reconstruction error) and PCA features generally do not beat neurons; supervised DAS subspaces beat neurons throughout (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard neuron dimensions are at least as good units as SAE or PCA features for aligning known causal variables, though supervised non-basis-aligned subspaces are better.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The reported causal-variable localization values are averages across layers and counterfactual datasets, with best-layer values also given; the paper states it did not conduct exhaustive hyperparameter searches. For arithmetic it says the evidence is at chance for Gemma-2 and only faint for Llama-3.1. These experiments concern causal-variable localization, not the attribution-graph method named in V5.
record.rows_left_out: No other neuron-dimension results in Table 3 were omitted. Results for the other featurizers and circuit-localization methods are excluded because they do not report outcomes for standard hidden-vector dimensions as the method under evaluation.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron poles or of job shares in Qwen3-32B.
No interpretability-share estimates across models or scale; no MoE or trillion-parameter models.
No vision models; no analysis of polysemantic examples or recursive generalization.
No architecture, regularization or tool-quality manipulation; no vision interpretability shares.

No attribution graphs with neuron-to-neuron edges. No direct comparison against a trained replacement model's reconstruction error in circuit discovery. Models are 0.5B–8B, not frontier-scale. Node-level circuits are penalised by the edge-weighted size metric, which confounds the neuron-versus-edge comparison.
No natural-language explanations from activating examples.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

missing.what: Neuron-level circuit faithfulness: NAP (CF) and NAP-IG (CF) CMD and CPR per model and task, with random and edge-level (EAP-IG) comparisons, on public and private test sets.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests' relation hinged on DBM rows that do not measure V5's construct; the real V5-relevant evidence is the omitted NAP results. The neuron-level circuit comparison is confounded by the weighted edge-count size metric, under which one neuron costs many edges; authors attribute poor node-level scores to this. Not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit neuron poles or estimate the shares with one job, two related jobs, or jobs not yet understood.
It does not measure those audit shares across models or scale.
It does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons or recursive generalization.
It does not estimate interpretability shares across vision architectures, tools, or regularization choices.

It tests standard dimensions as features for causal-variable localization, not attribution graphs; it does not test whether attribution graphs explain behavior without a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
It does not test explanations written from activating examples or evaluate their prediction of firing on new examples.
It does not score natural-language neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: The study's own circuit-localization results (NAP and NAP-IG at neuron granularity vs random and edge methods) bear on V5.

tranche.reason: A different method (neuron-granularity node circuits by attribution patching, scored by faithfulness) on the same question: do circuits in the model's own basis, with no replacement model, explain behaviour?

source_check.notes: No rows; all verdicts come from Tables 2, 14 and 17, whose flattened layout I placed by counting cells (Table 2's first column is InterpBench AUROC; one Random cell per table is displaced). MIB's 'neurons' are single dimensions of submodule outputs (size d_model), not MLP hidden units. Circuit size counts weighted edges, which the authors say penalises node circuits. The ARC failure is Llama-3.1 only.

statements.correction: Table 14 MCQA CPR: NAP 0.38 (Qwen-2.5), 1.47 (Gemma-2), 1.69 (Llama-3.1); NAP-IG 0.77, 1.71, 1.87; EAP-IG-inputs 1.16, 1.64, 1.05. Random is 0.26-0.32, or 0.25-0.32 because one Random cell is displaced in the text. Table 2 MCQA CMD: NAP 0.30-0.35, NAP-IG 0.18-0.33 vs random 0.68-0.74 and EAP-IG 0.05-0.14.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: DBM standard-dimension alignments on ARC (Easy) answer-token variables, MCQA answer-token variables, and the reported RAVEL attribute cases outside the weaker country-attribute results
reader_labels.reason: Standard hidden dimensions yield nontrivial causal-variable localization results; the authors say DBM on standard dimensions shows they can be useful units of analysis (r1, r2, r7, r8, r15, r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Ordering variables, arithmetic carry, IOI variables, and RAVEL country and language results
reader_labels.reason: Performance is weaker or task-dependent, with Gemma arithmetic described as at chance and Llama arithmetic as only faintly successful; the paper also reports DAS outperforming DBM overall. The study does not test attribution graphs or their reconstruction error (r3, r4, r5, r6, r9, r10, r11, r12, r13, r14, r16, r17, r18, r20).
